narration.en: Let us map what famous writers felt about being interviewed.

say.en: At the centre is the interview, a form that some love and many hate.
Lewis Carroll had a horror of interviewers and never consented.
Kipling called it immoral, a crime and an assault on the person.
H. G. Wells called it an ordeal, yet he later gave many interviews.
V. S. Naipaul felt some people are wounded and lose a part of themselves.
Saul Bellow compared interviews to thumbprints on his windpipe.

body.en: Silvester notes that the *interview* has been part of journalism for a little over a hundred and thirty years. Opinions about it vary sharply. Lewis Carroll had a horror of interviewers and never agreed to be interviewed. Rudyard Kipling condemned the interview as immoral and an assault on the person. H. G. Wells called it an ordeal, though he later gave many interviews. Saul Bellow compared interviews to thumbprints on his windpipe, and V. S. Naipaul felt some people are wounded by them and lose a part of themselves.

problem.en: What did Rudyard Kipling think of interviews?

steps.en: State his view: he thought interviewing was immoral.
Add his strong words: a crime, an assault on the person.
Mention the detail: reporters once spoiled a day for him and his wife.

answer.en: Kipling strongly disliked interviews. He called interviewing immoral, a crime and an assault on the person, and his wife recorded in her diary how two reporters from Boston had ruined their day.
